claims.text: The critical temperature of equiatomic Ti–V–Cr–Mo–W is predominantly governed by valence electron count.
Controlled elemental substitution changes the density of states at the Fermi level and thereby changes electron–phonon coupling.
The starting alloy is equiatomic Ti–V–Cr–Mo–W, so each element is present at 20 atomic percent.
Arc-melted equiatomic Ti–V–Cr–Mo–W forms a single-phase solid solution.
Replacing V with Nb increases the alloy's valence electron count.
Replacing V with Mn decreases the alloy's valence electron count.
Arc melting ensures a homogeneous solid solution.
Changing valence electron count shifts the Fermi level.
A Fermi-level shift modifies the density of states at the Fermi energy.
Changes in the Fermi-level density of states directly modify the electron–phonon coupling parameter.
Electron–phonon coupling is related to superconducting Tc within a BCS/McMillan description.
Increasing valence electron count will increase the density of states at the Fermi level.
A higher density of states will produce stronger electron–phonon coupling and a higher Tc.
A higher Fermi-level density of states will be accompanied by a higher low-temperature electronic specific-heat coefficient.
Decreasing valence electron count will lower Tc relative to equiatomic Ti–V–Cr–Mo–W.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Substitution levels of approximately 5–15 atomic percent are sufficiently low to avoid phase separation or significant structural changes.
Disorder or local structural fluctuations may mask the direct electronic effect on Tc.
Low-temperature electronic specific heat can be used to estimate the density of states at the Fermi level.
Absence of a systematic monotonic relationship among nominal electron count, measured density of states, and Tc would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed substitutions do not implement the stated electron-count directions: Nb and V are both group-5 elements under the usual valence-electron-count convention, while Mn has a higher, not lower, nominal valence electron count than V.

The predicted outcome says that lowering electron count should lower Tc, but the falsification rule's parenthetical wording treats a decrease in Tc at lower count as falsifying, even though that observation would agree with the prediction.
